mu-b889ed68.stem: Which is the only laryngeal muscle that opens the rima glottidis (abducts the vocal folds)?
mu-b889ed68.explanation: Posterior cricoarytenoid pulls the muscular processes of the arytenoids backwards, rotating the vocal processes outwards and opening the glottis. In bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury paralysis of these muscles leaves the vocal folds in the midline, with stridor and respiratory distress.
notes: It tenses the vocal folds; it does not open them.
It relaxes the vocal folds.
It brings the vocal folds together.
It draws the arytenoids together and closes the posterior glottis.

mu-19279b2e.stem: After total thyroidectomy a patient becomes hoarse. Laryngoscopy shows the left vocal fold immobile in the paramedian position. Which nerve has been damaged?
options: Internal branch of the left superior laryngeal nerve
Superior root of the ansa cervicalis
External branch of the left superior laryngeal nerve
mu-19279b2e.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid and lies close to the inferior thyroid artery. In unilateral injury the vocal fold stays in the paramedian position and the voice is hoarse. Injury to the external branch causes voice fatigue and difficulty with high notes; the internal branch is sensory.
notes: It carries sensation from the mucosa above the glottis; it is not motor.
It supplies the infrahyoid muscles.
It supplies the tongue muscles.
It supplies only cricothyroid.

mu-0d2b8196.stem: Which is the only pharyngeal muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve?
mu-0d2b8196.explanation: All the pharyngeal muscles are supplied by the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus; the only exception is stylopharyngeus, arising from the styloid process (glossopharyngeal nerve). It enters the pharynx between the superior and middle constrictors and raises the pharynx in swallowing.

mu-d0f50799.stem: Where is Killian's triangle, through which a Zenker diverticulum emerges?
options: Between the middle and inferior constrictors
Between the cricopharyngeal fibres and the longitudinal muscle layer of the oesophagus
Between the thyropharyngeal and cricopharyngeal fibres of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor
Between the superior and middle constrictors
Between stylopharyngeus and the superior constrictor
mu-d0f50799.explanation: Killian's triangle is the weak posterior area between the oblique thyropharyngeal fibres and the horizontal cricopharyngeal fibres (upper oesophageal sphincter) of the inferior constrictor. When the cricopharyngeal fibres fail to relax, the mucosa herniates backwards here. The area between cricopharyngeus and the oesophageal muscles is Laimer's triangle.

mu-4997b610.stem: Which muscle, lying deep to trapezius at the back of the neck, turns the head to the same side?
mu-4997b610.explanation: Splenius capitis arises from the nuchal ligament and upper thoracic spinous processes and attaches to the mastoid process and superior nuchal line; contracting on one side it turns the head to the same side. SCM turns the face to the opposite side; the two muscles work together in turning the head.
notes: It tilts the head to the same side and turns the face to the opposite side.
It bends the neck to the same side; it does not turn the head.
It elevates the scapula.
It turns the face to the opposite side.

mu-48308dfb.stem: Which muscles bound the suboccipital triangle?
options: Longissimus capitis, rectus capitis posterior major and obliquus capitis inferior
Rectus capitis posterior minor, obliquus capitis superior and inferior
Rectus capitis posterior minor and major, and obliquus capitis inferior
Semispinalis capitis, splenius capitis and obliquus capitis superior
Rectus capitis posterior major, obliquus capitis superior and obliquus capitis inferior
mu-48308dfb.explanation: The superomedial border of the triangle is rectus capitis posterior major, the superolateral border obliquus capitis superior and the inferior border obliquus capitis inferior. Its floor is the posterior arch of the atlas and posterior atlanto-occipital membrane; it contains the vertebral artery and suboccipital nerve; its roof is covered by semispinalis capitis.

mu-6c14a49e.stem: Which nerve supplies the suboccipital muscles?
options: Lesser occipital nerve (anterior ramus of C2)
Greater occipital nerve (posterior ramus of C2)
Third occipital nerve (posterior ramus of C3)
mu-6c14a49e.explanation: The suboccipital nerve, the posterior ramus of C1, emerges between the vertebral artery and the posterior arch of the atlas and supplies all the muscles of the suboccipital triangle; it usually has no cutaneous branch. The greater occipital nerve emerges below obliquus capitis inferior and supplies the skin of the back of the neck and scalp.
notes: It carries sensation from the skin behind the ear.
It carries sensation from the back of the neck and scalp; it does not supply the suboccipital muscles.
It supplies trapezius and SCM.
It supplies the skin of the lower back of the neck.

mu-141ea87a.stem: Which muscle turns the head to the same side and forms the inferior border of the suboccipital triangle?
mu-141ea87a.explanation: Obliquus capitis inferior, running from the spine of the axis to the transverse process of the atlas, is the only suboccipital muscle that does not attach to the skull; it rotates the atlas and head on the axis to the same side.

mu-ff99c4dc.stem: Which structures bound the triangle of auscultation?
options: Trapezius, latissimus dorsi and the medial border of the scapula
Latissimus dorsi, external oblique and iliac crest
Quadratus lumborum, 12th rib and internal oblique
Teres major, teres minor and the long head of triceps
mu-ff99c4dc.explanation: In the triangle of auscultation the muscle layer is thin; when the patient leans forwards and folds the arms, the scapula moves laterally, the triangle widens and lung sounds are heard better. The other options are the inferior lumbar (Petit), superior lumbar (Grynfeltt), posterior cervical triangles and the scapular spaces.

mu-d850fa84.stem: Which is the most lateral column of erector spinae?
mu-d850fa84.explanation: From lateral to medial erector spinae consists of the iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis columns ('I Love Spaghetti'). Multifidus and semispinalis belong to the deeper transversospinal group. All are supplied by the posterior rami of the spinal nerves.

mu-f74bf272.stem: Which transversospinal muscle is thickest in the lumbar region and plays an important role in segmental stabilisation?
mu-f74bf272.explanation: Multifidus extends from the sacrum to C2 and is thickest in the lumbar region; it binds each vertebra to the 2–4 below and stabilises the segments. Its wasting and fatty infiltration are common in chronic low back pain. Semispinalis is prominent in the thoracic–cervical region, rotatores in the thoracic region.

options: Medial border of the scapula, from the root of the spine to the inferior angle
The small part of the medial border of the scapula at the level of the spine
Along the medial border of the anterior surface of the scapula
mu-9657aa4e.explanation: Rhomboid major arises from the spinous processes of T2–T5 and inserts into the part of the medial border of the scapula below the spine; rhomboid minor runs from C7–T1 to the level of the root of the spine. Both are supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve and pull the scapula backwards and upwards.
notes: This is the insertion of pectoralis minor.
This is the insertion of rhomboid minor.
This is the insertion of levator scapulae.
This is the insertion of serratus anterior.

options: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C1–C4
Anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3–C6
Superior nuchal line and nuchal ligament
mu-7e7967a0.explanation: Levator scapulae arises from the upper cervical vertebrae and attaches to the superior angle and upper medial border of the scapula. It elevates the scapula and rotates it downwards; it is supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve and branches of C3–C4.

mu-5b14c6af.stem: Which of the following is NOT an action of latissimus dorsi?
options: Pulling the trunk up with the arms fixed
mu-5b14c6af.explanation: Latissimus dorsi attaches to the floor of the intertubercular sulcus; it extends, adducts and internally rotates the arm (the 'swimmer's muscle'). With the arms fixed (pull-up) it pulls the trunk upwards. External rotation is the job of infraspinatus and teres minor.
